extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of moral philosophy; readers studying Kant's Groundwork/Metaphysics of Morals
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and critique of pure practical reason in Kant's Groundwork/Metaphysics of Morals, addressing the nature of the moral law, the summum bonum, the antinomy of practical reason, and the primacy of practical over speculative reason. Aimed at clarifying principles that ground moral obligation, freedom, and the relation of virtue to happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral law as unconditioned causality
rubrics_metrics.description: An incontestable objective principle of causality which excludes all sensible conditions: a principle in which reason does not appeal further to something else as a determining ground of its causality, but contains this determining ground itself by means of that principle, and in which therefore it is itself as pure reason practical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identifies the moral law as a form of unconditioned causality grounded in freedom. From it follows that a being who is subject to the moral law (myself) belongs also to the supersensible world; thus the reality of the supersensible is established for practical purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of practical reason's knowledge of the supersensible
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical reason can help us to pass beyond the world of sense and give us knowledge of a supersensible order and connection, which, however, for this very reason cannot be extended further than is necessary for pure practical purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical reason yields knowledge of the supersensible only insofar as required for moral (practical) ends; it must not be used to support speculative claims beyond what is necessary for those ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological rigor and frankness in philosophical inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: In every scientific inquiry we should pursue our way steadily with all possible exactness and frankness, without caring for any objections that may be raised from outside its sphere, but, as far as we can, to carry out our inquiry truthfully and completely by itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should avoid prejudice and outside distractions, complete the internal investigation of principles, and not pre-judge results by extraneous doctrines. Kant notes that doubts in one part often reconcile with independent discoveries elsewhere if one proceeds honestly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid applying the idea of the unconditioned to appearances (dialectical caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the rational idea of the totality of the conditions (the unconditioned) to appearances gives rise to an inevitable illusion, as if appearances were things in themselves; this illusion betrays itself by a conflict of reason with itself (antinomies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One must perform a complete critical examination of the faculty of reason to trace and remove such illusions; the dialectic that produces antinomies, though an error, can be beneficial by driving us to such critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral law as sole determining principle of a pure will (autonomy vs heteronomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral law is the sole determining principle of a pure will. If we assume any object under the name of a good as a determining principle of the will prior to the moral law, this would introduce heteronomy and crush out the moral principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maxims must be determined by the moral law itself (autonomy). Treating objects (e.g., happiness) as prior determinants corrupts genuine morality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct conception of the summum bonum (supreme vs perfect good)
rubrics_metrics.description: The summum may mean either the supreme (supremum) or the perfect (consummatum). Virtue is the supreme condition of all that is desirable and thus the supreme good, but the whole and perfect good (summum bonum) for finite rational beings requires both virtue and happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish the logical sense (supremum) from the holistic/perfect sense (consummatum). The summum bonum of a possible world involves virtue as condition and happiness as its morally conditioned complement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between virtue and happiness must be synthetic (causal), not analytic
rubrics_metrics.description: The connection of virtue and happiness cannot be analytically known (they are specifically distinct); it must be synthetical and conceived as a connection of cause and effect: either pursuit of happiness as motive to virtue (impossible morally) or virtue producing happiness (also problematic in the sensible world).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the unity of virtue and happiness cannot be deduced by mere analysis, their necessary combination for the summum bonum requires a synthetic (a priori moral) grounding, which leads to the antinomy needing resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution of the antinomy of practical reason via noumenal freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: The apparent contradiction (that virtue should necessarily produce happiness vs that it cannot) is resolved by distinguishing the same agent as appearance (phenomenon) with causality according to nature and as noumenon (intelligible being) that can be the seat of a principle free from laws of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By positing the intelligible/noumenal aspect of the agent (freedom), morality can be causally connected to happiness in a way not available within the empirical order alone (e.g., through an intelligent author of nature or noumenal order).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of the pursuit of happiness cannot produce morality
rubrics_metrics.description: Maxims which place the determining principle of the will in the desire of personal happiness are not moral at all; principles of the pursuit of happiness cannot possibly produce morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral motivation must come from duty and the law, not from expected pleasurable outcomes. Seeking to ground morality in prudential aims introduces heteronomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consciousness of moral determination yields intellectual contentment, not sensible pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Consciousness that the will is determined directly by the law is the source of a satisfaction in the resulting action (self-contentment) which is not the same as sensible pleasure; respect, not pleasure, is the proper response of reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish the intellectual contentment (negative satisfaction, self-contentment) that accompanies moral action from contingent sensible happiness; do not reframe the moral spring as mere pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclinations (even benevolent) must not be the determining principle of moral action
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclination is blind and slavish, whether of a good sort or not, and when morality is in question, reason must not play the part merely of guardian to inclination; compassionate feelings that precede deliberation and determine action undermine proper moral maxims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maxims should be directed to the conception of the law as determining principle; inclinations may facilitate but cannot constitute moral principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of practical reason in union with speculative reason
rubrics_metrics.description: When pure speculative and pure practical reason are combined in one cognition, the latter has the primacy, provided this combination is founded a priori on reason itself and therefore necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speculative reason should accept practical a priori propositions when they are inseparably attached to the practical interest and do not contradict speculative principles; practical reason's interest (determination of the will toward final ends) is supreme in combined employment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy/wisdom as an ideal requiring exemplification
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy as love of wisdom remains an ideal; a teacher of wisdom implies more than a scholar and must be able to show the infallible effects of wisdom in his own person (self-mastery and pre-eminent interest in the general good).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One should be modest about claiming the title 'philosopher' unless one can exemplify the moral fruits of wisdom; the definition itself demurs against self-conceit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty in stating dialectical contradictions promotes critical progress
rubrics_metrics.description: The self-contradictions of pure practical reason honestly stated, and not concealed, force us to undertake a complete critique of this faculty; the antinomy thus becomes a beneficial error driving inquiry to discover corrective principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not hide contradictions; exposing them enables a critical solution and can reveal previously unsuspected necessary principles (e.g., noumenal considerations).
